name: Underhand Lat Pulldown

inherit.field: grip.handContact (handle across the base of the fingers and top edge of the palm, like carrying a bag)
inherit.why: true for this child because the cable pulls across the fingers exactly as on the lat_pulldown bar; only the handle or palm direction changes.

inherit.field: grip.thumb (wrapped by default; thumb over the handle allowed as a comfort option)
inherit.why: true for this child because, as on the parent, the handle cannot fall on the lifter, so thumb position is a comfort choice with the wrapped grip as default.

inherit.field: setup: weight set and pin pushed all the way in; start lighter than you think
inherit.why: true for this child because it is the same selector-stack machine.

inherit.field: posture: bar comes down in front of the face, never behind the head
inherit.why: true for this child because an underhand bar can only be pulled to the front; the parent's front-path evidence applies unchanged.

inherit.field: zooms: seat height / thigh pad crop
inherit.why: true for this child because the pad setting is identical (c4).

claims.text: Take the bar underhand (palms facing you), about shoulder-width apart, standing, then sit down.

quotes.text: Stand up and grip the bar with an underhand grip (palms facing towards you) about shoulder width apart, then sit down.

claims.text: A second coach source sets the hands a little closer than shoulder width and allows a wrapped or thumbless grip.

quotes.text: Grab the bar a little bit closer than shoulder-width apart with your palms facing you. You can choose to wrap your thumb around the bar or use a thumbless grip.

claims.text: Coach opinion: with palms facing you, a closer grip is likely less strain on the shoulders than a wide one.

quotes.text: That’s likely because it’s less strain on your shoulders for your forearms to be supinated (palms facing you) when they’re closer together.

claims.text: Set the pads tight against the thighs.

quotes.text: Sit down on the lat pulldown machine and adjust the pads so they sit tightly against your thighs.

claims.text: Lean back only slightly, no more than about 30 degrees, and add no extra lean during the pull.

quotes.text: Lean back slightly (no more than a 30 degree angle), using your legs to support your body (low back).
Avoid any additional backwards lean during the pull movement.

claims.text: Pull the elbows back and down toward the glutes and stop when the bar passes just below chin height.

quotes.text: Lower the bar towards your chest by pulling your elbows back and down towards the glutes, stopping when the bar passes just below chin height.

claims.text: Avoid momentum and keep the torso stable while the elbows pull down and back.

quotes.text: It’s important to avoid using momentum to pull the bar down so that the correct muscles are engaged. Think about keeping your torso stable

claims.text: Pulling the bar further down lets the forearms and front shoulders take over (coach source).

quotes.text: Pulling the bar further down forces your forearms and deltoids to take over, shifting the load away from your lats and biceps.

claims.text: Return slowly with control; if you can't control the bar on the way up, the weight is too heavy.

quotes.text: Reverse the movement by slowly extending the arms, allowing the cable to pull the bar back up with control.
If you don’t have any control of the bar when it rises back to the top position, you’re likely lifting too heavy.

claims.text: Start the pull by drawing the shoulder blades down, then pull.

quotes.text: initiate the downward pull by first depressing (lower) your scapulae

claims.text: Stop pulling once the elbows stop moving down and start moving back; ACE says further pulling adds stress to the shoulder joint. Written for the overhand bar; applied here because the elbow path is the same.

quotes.text: Continue pulling until the bar nears or touches your chest, or more importantly, you observe your elbows no longer moving downward, but now beginning to move backwards.
Avoid any further pulling as this places additiomnal stresses into the shoulder joint.

claims.text: Lusk 2010 tested underhand and overhand pulldowns at a 2-second pull and a 2-second return; the plate uses that cadence. It is a study protocol, not a tested recommendation.

quotes.text: Participants maintained a cadence of 2-second concentric and 2-second eccentric phases.

claims.text: Measured with EMG in 12 men, the overhand grip gave more lat activity than the underhand grip, and grip type did not change biceps or middle-trapezius activity.

quotes.text: a pronated grip elicited greater LD activity than a supinated grip (p < 0.05), but had no influence of grip type on the MT and BB muscles.

claims.text: In a 10-man EMG study the underhand (supinated) grip gave less lat activity than a wide overhand grip to the front.

quotes.text: During the concentric phase, NrmsEMG results for the LD included WGA > WGP, SG, CG.

claims.text: In 40 trained men, lat activity did not differ significantly across seven pulldown grips, widths and lean angles.

quotes.text: These findings suggest that grip variations may not significantly alter latissimus dorsi recruitment

claims.text: Coaches say the underhand grip puts more emphasis on the biceps (not confirmed by the EMG in c13).

quotes.text: By reversing your grip, you’re putting a lot more emphasis on your biceps.

claims.text: Coach source: it works the lats, rhomboids, traps, rear delts and biceps.

quotes.text: Reverse grip lat pulldowns work the back muscles, including the lats, rhomboids, traps, as well as the rear delts and biceps.

claims.text: Grip strength drops when the wrist moves 10 to 15 degrees away from its self-chosen position, so a curled or bent wrist costs grip (hand dynamometer, applied here by reasoning).

quotes.text: Grip strength was significantly less in any position of deviation from this self-selected position, even after accounting for fatigue.

sources.title: How to Do the Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldown for Stronger Back and Biceps (BarBend)
Electromyographic Analysis of Back Muscle Activation During Lat Pulldown Exercise: Effects of Grip Variations and Forearm Orientation (Buonsenso et al., J Funct Morphol Kinesiol)
Grip width and forearm orientation effects on muscle activity during the lat pull-down (Lusk, Hale, Russell, J Strength Cond Res)
The relationship between wrist position, grasp size, and grip strength (O'Driscoll et al., J Hand Surg Am)
Reverse Grip Lat Pulldown (PureGym exercise guide)
A comparative electromyographical investigation of muscle utilization patterns using various hand positions during the lat pull-down (Signorile, Zink, Szwed, J Strength Cond Res)

plate.equipment: Lat pulldown station and long bar, as the parent plate; hands underhand about shoulder width (c1).
plate.start: Seated, thighs tight under the pad (c4); arms straight overhead, underhand grip about shoulder width (c1); slight lean, no more than about 30 degrees (c5); shoulder blades drawn down to begin (c10).
plate.end: Bar just below the chin, elbows pulled down and back toward the glutes (c6); torso lean unchanged (c5, c7).

checkpoints.label: Elbows down, back
checkpoints.what: Elbows pull down and back toward the glutes.

checkpoints.label: Bar below chin
checkpoints.what: Stop when the bar passes just below chin height.

mistake.what: Using momentum: the torso rocks back to drive the bar down, then swings forward as it rises.
mistake.why: The coach source names momentum first and asks for a stable torso; ACE limits the lean to about 30 degrees with no extra lean during the pull. Frequency is not measured.

tells.text: Bar stops just below the chin

grip.width: About shoulder width, or a little closer; closer is likely easier on the shoulders.
grip.thumb: Wrapped by default (inherited); thumbless is a coach-allowed option.
grip.handContact: Inherited from lat_pulldown: bar across the base of the fingers.
grip.wrist: Straight, not curled; a bent wrist costs grip.

setup.step: Sit and set the pads tight against your thighs.
Stand, take the bar underhand about shoulder width, then sit down.
Lean back slightly, no more than about 30 degrees.
Draw your shoulder blades down to start the pull.

posture.point: Torso stable; the lean does not change.
Elbows down and back toward the glutes.
Stop just below the chin, when the elbows stop moving down.
Slow, controlled return to straight arms.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Rocking the torso to swing the bar down.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep the torso still. If you can't, lower the weight.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Pulling the bar down to the belly.
handlingMistakes.fix: Stop when the bar passes just below your chin.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Letting the bar fly back up.
handlingMistakes.fix: Control it all the way up; if you can't, the weight is too heavy.

rows.means: Common with this grip; coaches say it works the biceps more, though EMG found no biceps difference between grips.
rows.fix: Nothing to fix. Keep leading with the elbows.

rows.means: Usually means you are pulling the bar too low.
Usually means the grip is too wide for palms facing you, or you pull past the stop point.
rows.fix: Bring the hands in to about shoulder width and stop when the elbows stop moving down. If it still hurts, stop and get it checked.

rows.means: Usually means you are rocking the weight down.
rows.fix: Keep the lean slight and still, and lower the weight.

risks.risk: Shoulder stress from pulling past the point where the elbows stop moving down.

zooms.right: Palms facing you, bar across the base of the fingers, wrists straight.
zooms.wrong: Wrists bent back under the bar, grip opening.

zooms.right: Slight fixed lean, bar just below the chin.
zooms.wrong: Torso thrown back well past 30 degrees to drive the bar down.

add.why: Listed by the coach source (c17); no EMG for this grip beyond Signorile's posterior-deltoid data.

libraryDiff.why: lats primary and biceps and mid_back secondary stand. The underhand grip is not better for the lats (c13, c14) and grip may not matter much (c15).

notes: PureGym's claims that the underhand grip lets most people lift more and may suit people prone to shoulder pain are not used: no measured source was found for either, and the chin_up card records shoulder-risk kinematics for a palms-toward-you hang. BarBend's full reverse-grip guide was also read in full.
